latin: Regulus. — Solem occidentem spectare cupio... Gratum mihi feceris si solem occidere jusseris.
Rex. — Si ducem<sup>1</sup>, papilionis more, circum flosculos<sup>2</sup> volitare, vel tragoediam scribere, vel se in marinam avem<sup>3</sup> convertere juberem...
dux autem imperatum non faceret, utrius vitium esset<sup>4</sup> meum an ejus?
Reg., constanti voce. — Tuum!
Rex. — Recte dicis. Tantum enim ab unoquoque exigendum est, quantum<sup>5</sup> dare unusquisque potest*.
Nempe auctoritas in ratione nititur<sup>6</sup>.
Si populares tuos juberes se in mare abjicere, rem publicam commutarent<sup>7</sup>.
Reg. — Quid igitur de meo solis occasu? (nunquam enim omittebat quod semel quaesiverat).
Rex. — Occasus solis iste tibi dabitur. Exigam<sup>8</sup> enim. Sed ut qui rei publicae ministrandae peritus sim, tempus exspectabo.
Reg. — Quota hora id futurum est?
Rex, postquam ingentes fastos<sup>9</sup> inspexit. — Hem! Hem!... Hem! Hem!... fiet* hodie vespere... fiet... quadragesima minuta post septimam horam,
ac videbis quam mihi sedulo pareatur...
Reg. — Nihil jam mihi negotii hic est. Mox proficiscar.
Rex. — Noli proficisci!
Reg. — O, summe rex, si tibi sedulo oboediri<sup>10</sup> cupis, mihi rationi consentanea impera. Me proficisci jube. Omnia enim tempestiva videntur esse.
Rex, regulum jam evolantem videns. — Te legatum<sup>11</sup> meum esse jubeo!
english: The little prince. — I want to see the setting sun... You would make me grateful if you [ordered] (will have ordered) the sun to set.
The king. — If I ordered a general to flutter around the flowers in the manner of a butterfly, or to write a tragedy, or to change himself into a seabird...
and if the general did not carry out the order, [whose] would the fault be, mine or his?
The prince, in a firm voice. — Yours!
The king. — You are right. [As much] (so much) must be demanded of each one [as each one] (as much as each one) can give.
First of all, authority rests on reason.
If you ordered your fellow citizens to throw themselves into the sea, they would make the revolution.
The prince. — Then, [what about] (what of) my sunset? (for he never forgot a question once [he had asked it] (he had asked)).

The king. — This sunset, [it] will be given to you. For I will demand it. But as [I know well] (who be skilful in the administration of the republic) [the science of government], I will wait for the [opportune] moment.
The prince. — At what time will it take place?
The king, after consulting an enormous calendar. — Hem! Hem!... [it] will be (made) [this evening] (today evening)... it will be... at seven forty (40 min. after 7 h.),
and you will see how I am obeyed docilely...
The prince. — [I have nothing more to do here] (nothing henceforth to me of business here is), I will (soon) leave.
The king. — Don't leave!

The prince. — O very great king, if you want to be obeyed docilely, [give] (to) me [a reasonable order] (things in conformity with reason command). Order me to leave. Everything in fact seems favourable.
The king, seeing the little prince [going away] (already flying away). — I order you to be my ambassador!

footnotes: Dux, ducis, m., the chief, the guide; Italian duce (pr. doutché).
Flosculus: diminutive of flos, floris, m., and masculine like the latter.
Avis, -is, f.: to remember its gender, think of rara avis, the rare bird (same ironic sense as in English).

Si jubeam, mihi vitium sit, PRESENT POTENTIAL, if I ordered, I would be wrong (I can order, I am free to do so or not to do so): in Latin, PRESENT SUBJUNCTIVE. Si juberem, mihi vitium esset = PRESENT UNREAL (same translation); but in Latin the use of the IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE (past of the infectum) makes it possible to specify that it is an unreal supposition in the present (as seems to be the case here!). Si jussissem, mihi vitium fuisset = PAST UNREAL, if I had ordered, I would have been wrong (but in any case I did not order): in Latin, PLUPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE (past of the perfectum). Note further that faceret (P. 3) is also in the imperfect subjunctive (si is understood).
Nitor, -eris, -i, nisus sum + abl., to lean on (vid. L. 71, exercise). It also means to make an effort, to strive to: niti ad gloriam, to strive towards glory.
Commutare = cum + mutare, to change completely; whence commutare rem publicam, to change the republic, that is to say to make the revolution.
Fasti, -orum, m. pl., the «fasti» days, during which the tribunals held audience, whence the table which indicates them, that is to say the calendar. — Ingens, -entis, adj., immense.
Oboedire = ob audire (4th conjugation), to lend an ear; whence to obey.
Legare, to delegate; not to be confused with legere, to read. Legatus, the delegate, the ambassador. The legate is the delegate (the lieutenant) of a general.
comments: Ignis, -is, m., fire; think of igneous, ignifuge, etc. — Norit*, abridged form of noverit, perfect subjunctive of nosse* (novisse).

latin: Qua in arte te exerces?
Ego sum centurio e sparteolis urbanis.
Quale est ministerium tuum? — Sparteolis impero ut incendia exstinguant.
Saepene in hac urbe incendia exstinguis?
Nimis saepe! In aedibus nostris contabulationes ligneae, supellex, vela, textilia, facile incenduntur.
Homines praecipueque mulieres cum igne incaute saepissime agunt.
Machinasne recentes possidetis?
Duas habemus antlias autocinetas optimas.
In utramvis aurem nunc dormiam, qui urbis nostrae sparteolos, te duce, optime instructos esse, nunc non ignoro.
Et tu, bone, quo ministerio fungeris?
Ego libitinarius sum.
Optime! Sine ullo tandem timore ad ignem exstinguendum adire* possum, quia scio a te me bene sepultum iri.
Quam quisque norit* artem, in hac se exerceat.
english: [What is your job] (in what job do you exercise)?
I am captain [of the] [town] (urban) firemen.
[What does] your [job consist of]? — I command the firemen [to put out] the fires.
Do you often put out fires in this town?
Too often! In our houses the wooden floors, the furniture, the curtains, the fabrics [catch fire] (are set alight) easily.
Men and above all women very often [act imprudently] with fire.
Do you have modern equipment?
We have two excellent motor fire pumps.
I'll sleep on [both] (either) ear[s] now [that] I know that the firemen of our town, with you [as] chief, are perfectly equipped.
And you, my good man, [what is your job] (in what function are you invested)?
Me, I'm an undertaker.
Very good! At last I can go and put out fires without the slightest fear, for I know that I will be well buried by you.
Let each one exercise himself in the trade he knows (= each to his own trade... and the cows will be well guarded).
